phonemes.desc: Syllable with high front glide [j] (written 'y' in Pinyin), high front vowel [i], alveolar nasal [n], and Tone 1 (high level, ˥).
Syllable with glide [j], open vowel [a], velar nasal [ŋ], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). The final '-ng' is a single velar nasal, not a cluster.

pronunciation.approximation: YIN-YAHNG — first syllable high and level, second syllable rising from mid to high.

pronunciation.note: 陰陽 (Yīnyáng) denotes the complementary cosmic dualities—dark/passive/female and bright/active/male—central to Daoist cosmology, traditional Chinese medicine, and the Yijing. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is yīn (Tone 1) + yáng (Tone 2), as given in the Unihan Database (kMandarin). For historical context, Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 陰 as *q(r)um (GSR 0651y, 'dark') and 陽 as *laŋ (GSR 0720e, 'bright'). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Yīnyáng accurately preserves the citation tones.

domains.title: The Two Modes
domains.subtitle: Complementary Cosmic Duality
domains.lead:
Yīnyáng is not a battle between good and evil. It is the Chinese understanding that every phenomenon is shaped by the pull of two complementary tendencies: dark and bright, still and active, receptive and assertive, earth and heaven. The earliest meanings of the words were topographical — yīn the shady north side of a hill, yáng the sunny south side — and from that concrete root grew a cosmology that underlies medicine, statecraft, martial arts, and divination.

What makes yin and yang powerful is not their opposition but their interdependence. Each contains a seed of the other, and each turns into the other at its extreme.

cards.name: Darkness and Light
cards.desc: Yin is not merely dark; it is the capacity to receive, to hold, to rest. Yang is not merely bright; it is the capacity to act, to extend, to warm.

cards.name: Cyclic Transformation
cards.desc: At its height, yang becomes yin; at its depth, yin becomes yang. This is the engine of seasons, days, and human fortunes.

cards.name: Cosmic Balance
cards.desc: Health, harmony, and good government all depend on keeping yin and yang in dynamic equilibrium rather than crushing one side.

cards.name: Medical Diagnosis
cards.desc: Traditional Chinese medicine reads illness as yin-yang imbalance: too much heat, too little moisture, excess above, deficiency below.

mythology.lead: Yīnyáng has no origin myth in the usual sense. It is a lens through which Chinese thinkers read the origin of everything. Its stories are therefore cosmological and medical rather than biographical — a sequence of texts, from divination manual to Daoist classic to Han statecraft, each of which made the pair do more work.

myths.title: One Yin, One Yang
myths.text: The Xici — the Appended Statements, the philosophical commentary attached to the Yijing by the third century BCE — comes as close to a creed as the tradition allows: 'One yin and one yang: this is called the Dao' (Xici, Part A, §5). The cosmos, in this reading, is not governed by a personal deity but by the alternation of two modes, and the hexagrams of the classic are nothing more than snapshots of that alternation — sixty-four positions in the endless turning. Divination is therefore not fortune-telling but diagnosis: the stalks are cast to learn where one stands in the cycle, and the answer assumes that knowing the pattern is enough to act within it. It is one of the great minimalist creation accounts: the world needs no maker if it has rhythm, and no judge if imbalance announces itself as disorder. The Yijing gives the pair its earliest full metaphysics — and never once asks who set the rhythm going.

myths.title: All Things Carry Yin and Embrace Yang
myths.text: The Daodejing (ch. 42) compresses the whole cosmogony into nine characters of arithmetic: 'The Dao gives birth to One; the One gives birth to Two; the Two give birth to Three; the Three give birth to the ten thousand things.' Then it locates the pair inside every creature: 'The ten thousand things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang in their arms, and achieve harmony by blending the empty breath' (chongqi). Yin and yang are thus not external forces but the internal structure of existence — every thing is a standing negotiation between its dark and its light, and harmony is not a state but a blending, a continual mixing of the vital breath. Where the Yijing watches the pair from outside, the Daodejing finds it within: creation is not manufacture but equilibrium, and the world is not a machine made once but a chord kept sounding.

myths.title: The Physician of Qin Reads the Six Qi
myths.text: By the sixth century BCE, yin-yang had become clinical. The Zuo Zhuan (Duke Zhao, year 1, 541 BCE) preserves what may be the first case history in Chinese literature: the ruler of Jin lies ill, and the court proposes ghosts and spoiled food as causes; the physician He, summoned from Qin, rejects both. Illness, he says, comes from the imbalance of the six qi of heaven — yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and light — which descend to produce the five flavors, the five colors, and the five tones, and which, when any one runs to excess, disorder the body. He names the ruler's own excesses as the diagnosis. The scene matters because it is argumentative: a physician lecturing a duke that his sickness has a natural, impersonal mechanism — qi, not curse — and a lifestyle for a remedy. Yin-yang thought enters world literature not as mysticism but as the first rational medicine, and its founding document is a doctor politely telling a king the truth.

myths.title: The Han Synthesis
myths.text: In the second century BCE, Dong Zhongshu — chief scholar of Emperor Wu's court — welded yin-yang cosmology onto Confucian statecraft in the Chunqiu fanlu ('Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn'). Heaven, humanity, and state now formed a single responding body: the treatises on cosmic resonance (ganying) argued that droughts, eclipses, and earthquakes were heaven's admonitions to a misgoverning ruler, and the paired treatises on yin and yang gave the mechanism — the cosmic duality running through seasons, music, punishments, and rites alike, each side with its proper season and sphere. The theory made cosmology into a constitution: the emperor ruled under heaven's critique, and the scholar's job was to read the weather as the minutes of heaven's review. It is the most consequential application the pair ever received — and its double edge is visible from the start. The same doctrine that let remonstrating officials argue against the throne also taught that harmony meant hierarchy, yang honored and yin in its place. Yin-yang became the grammar of empire, for emperors and for their critics alike.

lore.syncretism: Yīnyáng traveled with Chinese civilization into Korea (eum-yang), Japan (in'yō), and Vietnam (âm-dương), where it shaped local medicine, martial arts, and geomancy. In the early modern West, Leibniz saw in the Yijing's broken and solid lines a precursor to binary arithmetic, while Hegel read yin and yang as an early dialectic. Contemporary New Age culture has turned yin-yang into a universal emblem of balance, often severed from its technical roles in medicine and divination. The symbol also appears in Unicode as ☯ (U+262F), one of the most widely recognized non-Western glyphs in digital culture.
lore.culturalLegacy: Every acupuncture needle, feng shui compass, and tai chi form is a working application of yin-yang theory. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, diagnosis begins by asking whether a symptom is hot or cold, deficient or excess, interior or exterior, yin or yang. Martial artists use yin to absorb and yang to strike. Architects orient buildings to capture yang light and yin shade. The concept has also entered global popular culture as a shorthand for balance, duality, and counterculture — surfacing in music, fashion, tattoo art, and even psychology, where 'shadow' work loosely parallels the yin within yang. Yet the most rigorous legacy remains clinical: yin-yang is still the organizing axis of a living medical tradition.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Yīnyáng is an invitation to stop choosing sides. It says that what looks like opposition is really relationship: day has no meaning without night, speaking has no meaning without silence, strength has no meaning without vulnerability. The small dot in each half of the taijitu is the most radical part of the symbol: nothing is pure; everything carries the seed of its seeming opposite.

This is not relativism. Yin and yang are real, measurable, and consequential — but they are not moral categories. To call something yin is not to demean it; to call something yang is not to praise it. The question is always one of balance: too much yang burns, too much yin stagnates. The wise move, in medicine as in life, is to notice which way the scales are tipping and to restore the dynamic exchange.

lore.archaeology: The oldest layer of yin-yang thought is embedded in the Yijing itself, transmitted through Warring States bamboo and silk manuscripts such as the Mawangdui silk Yijing (c. 168 BCE) and the Guodian Chu slips (c. 300 BCE). The Zuo Zhuan preserves early medical and astrological uses of yin-yang terminology, while Han dynasty tomb texts and visual art pair the two principles with the Four Spirits and the five phases. The iconic two-tone taijitu diagram is a Song-era visual innovation, though the conceptual pairing it depicts is ancient.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 陰陽 in traditional Chinese and 阴阳 in simplified. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Yīnyáng (Tone 1 + Tone 2). The domain label yīn-yáng.com inserts an ASCII hyphen between the syllables for readability and registrability; this is a DNS convention and does not alter the Pinyin. The tone marks are preserved so the restoration remains phonetically accurate. Baxter & Sagart reconstruct 陰 as *q(r)um and 陽 as *laŋ.
